1. Introduction & Anatomy

Tintinalli Ch.152 p.1005
  • Skin and soft-tissue infections (SSTI) account for >4 million ED visits annually in the US, ~20× more often outpatient than admitted.
  • Spectrum: simple cellulitis → cutaneous abscess → necrotizing soft-tissue infection (life-threatening).
  • Anatomic key: depth of infection guides management. Superficial (epidermis/dermis) = impetigo, erysipelas; subcutaneous tissue = cellulitis; below fascia = necrotizing fasciitis.

Definitions

TermDescription
CellulitisInfection of dermis + subcutaneous tissue. Purulent (drainage/abscess) vs nonpurulent.
ErysipelasSuperficial cellulitis variant — lymphatic involvement, sharply demarcated raised border, "peau d'orange" appearance.
FolliculitisInfection at hair follicle — superficial.
Furuncle (boil)Infection extending into subcutaneous tissue from hair follicle.
CarbuncleCluster of furuncles draining via multiple skin openings.
Necrotizing fasciitis (NSTI)Rapidly progressive infection of fascia, subcutaneous tissue, sometimes muscle — surgical emergency.
📚 Fig 152-1 — Skin architecture: epidermis, dermis (papillary + reticular), subcutaneous tissue, with vascular plexuses (Tintinalli p.1005)

2. Cellulitis & Erysipelas

Tintinalli p.1005–1006

Microbiology

  • Most common cause: gram-positive bacteria, predominantly Staphylococcus aureus (including community-acquired MRSA).
  • Beta-hemolytic streptococci (Group A strep) — typically cause non-purulent cellulitis and erysipelas.
  • Erysipelas: classically caused by β-hemolytic strep. Bullous variant may have synergistic strep + S. aureus.
📚 Table 152-1 — General Risk Factors for Cellulitis and Erysipelas (Tintinalli p.1006)
📚 Table 152-2 — Risk Factors for Specific Organisms Causing Cellulitis (Tintinalli p.1006)

Clinical Features

FeatureCellulitisErysipelas
OnsetGradual over daysAcute, within 1–2 days
BorderIndistinct, "peau d'orange"Sharply demarcated, raised
Skin involvementDermis + subcutaneousSuperficial dermis + lymphatics
Fever / chillsCommonCommon
SiteLower extremities most commonFace, lower extremities
LymphangitisSometimesOften (red streaks)
📚 Fig 152-2 — Cellulitis of the right leg with erythema and mild swelling (Tintinalli p.1006)
📚 Fig 152-3 — Butterfly rash of erysipelas with sharp demarcation between salmon-red erythema and normal skin (Tintinalli p.1007)
Pearl — "peau d'orange": orange-peel skin appearance from edema around hair follicles. Classic for erysipelas (and a clue for inflammatory breast cancer in another context).

Answer: C. Erysipelas has a sharply demarcated, raised border. Cellulitis has indistinct edges. Reference: Tintinalli p.1006, Fig 152-3.

3. MRSA Considerations

Tintinalli p.1006
  • Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is now the most common cause of purulent SSTI in many US regions — irrespective of the patient's traditional risk factors.
  • Risk factors that strongly favor MRSA empiric therapy:
    • Purulent drainage or suspected/confirmed abscess
    • Prior MRSA infection or known colonization
    • Prior hospitalization or surgery within past year
    • Hemodialysis
    • Residence in long-term care facility
    • Crowded living environments (military barracks, prisons, dormitories)
    • Contact sports, MSM (men who have sex with men), IV drug use
    • Patient with suspected spider bite (often misidentified MRSA)
  • Nonpurulent cellulitis remains predominantly streptococcal — culture-negative; β-lactam therapy still appropriate.
Patient education pearl: patients (and clinicians) often mistake MRSA furuncles for "spider bites" — true spider bites are very rare; question the assumption when you see a "spider bite."

4. Diagnosis & Differential

Tintinalli Table 152-3 p.1007

Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Lab and imaging support but rarely confirm.

Workup considerations

  • Mild disease: no labs needed.
  • Moderate–severe disease: CBC, basic chemistry, lactate, blood cultures (rarely positive in simple cellulitis but indicated in toxic-appearing patients), CRP.
  • Wound culture not recommended for nonpurulent cellulitis but useful for purulent collections at I&D.
  • POCUS (ultrasound): useful to differentiate cellulitis (cobblestone appearance) vs abscess (anechoic fluid collection); also guides drainage.
  • Imaging: plain X-ray to look for gas in soft tissues; CT/MRI for suspected NSTI or deep abscess.
  • Doppler US to exclude DVT in lower-extremity cellulitis if uncertain.

Differential Diagnosis

📚 Table 152-3 — Differential Diagnosis of Cellulitis and Erysipelas (Tintinalli p.1007)
Important mimics to know:
  • DVT — typically no erythema/fever; warmth and swelling.
  • Stasis dermatitis — bilateral, chronic, mild tenderness, no fever.
  • Contact dermatitis — pruritus rather than pain; nontoxic appearance.
  • Necrotizing soft-tissue infection — pain out of proportion to exam, rapid progression, hemorrhagic bullae, systemic toxicity.
Inline MCQ 2. Which is the best initial bedside test to distinguish cellulitis from a drainable abscess?

Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.

Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. CT scan
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Blood culture
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. POCUS reliably differentiates cellulitis (cobblestone) from abscess (anechoic collection) and guides drainage. Reference: Tintinalli p.1007.

5. Treatment of Cellulitis

Tintinalli Tables 152-4, 152-5 p.1007–1009

General measures (all severity)

  • Elevation of affected area
  • Drainage of any abscess present (essential)
  • Treat predisposing conditions (tinea pedis = portal of entry)
  • Mark the leading edge with a pen — track progression

Purulent cellulitis (suspected MRSA)

📚 Table 152-4 — Empiric Treatment for Purulent Cellulitis or Suspected MRSA (Tintinalli p.1007)
SeverityFirst-line
Mild (oral)Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1–2 DS PO BID OR doxycycline 100 mg PO BID; clindamycin alternative
Moderate (IV)Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h OR linezolid 600 mg IV/PO BID
SevereVancomycin + broad-spectrum (piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem) per institutional protocol

Nonpurulent cellulitis / Erysipelas (likely streptococcal)

📚 Table 152-5 — Empiric Treatment of Nonpurulent Cellulitis/Erysipelas (Tintinalli p.1009)
SeverityFirst-line
Mild (oral)Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID OR dicloxacillin 500 mg PO QID
Moderate (IV)Cefazolin 1 g IV q8h OR ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily
Severe (with sepsis)Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem; consider necrotizing fasciitis
Penicillin allergy: use clindamycin (covers both strep and MRSA) for non-anaphylactic; use cephalosporin if reaction was rash only and not type I; vancomycin or linezolid if true severe penicillin allergy.

6. Cutaneous Abscess

Tintinalli p.1008–1010

Diagnosis

  • Clinical features: tender, fluctuant mass; central pustule may be visible.
  • POCUS useful for confirmation, especially in obese patients or deeper sites.
  • Differentiate from cellulitis (no fluid collection) and pseudoaneurysm (pulsatile mass — DON'T incise!).
📚 Fig 152-4 — Subcutaneous abscess in the axilla (Tintinalli p.1009)
📚 Fig 152-5 — Long-axis sonogram of a deep midline subcutaneous abscess (buttock); cavity is hyperechoic with surrounding edema (Tintinalli p.1010)

Incision & Drainage Procedure

  1. Universal precautions — eye protection, gown.
  2. Local anesthesia — slow infiltration of the wall; less pain than central injection.
  3. #11 blade incision over the apex of fluctuance.
  4. Express purulent material; loculated cavity may need probing/breaking with hemostat.
  5. Irrigate with NS.
  6. Pack with gauze (for larger abscesses) — controversial; small abscesses may be treated without packing.
  7. Wound check in 2–3 days; remove packing.
  8. Some advocate Loop drainage technique as alternative — vessel loop through 2 small incisions, removed in 7–10 days.
When NOT to drain in the ED:
  • Suspected pulsatile mass (pseudoaneurysm)
  • Deep neck or central facial infections (consult ENT/maxillofacial)
  • Very deep abscesses (consider IR drainage)
  • Periorbital, paronychia in pediatric, or sites near critical structures

Antibiotics adjunct after I&D?

  • Most simple abscesses: I&D alone is sufficient.
  • Adjunctive antibiotics improve cure when:
    • Abscess ≥2 cm
    • Surrounding cellulitis
    • Multiple abscesses
    • Immunocompromised host
    • Failed initial I&D
  • First-line oral: TMP-SMX 1–2 DS BID or doxycycline 100 mg BID.

7. Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infections (NSTI)

Tintinalli p.1010–1011

Definition & types

TypeMicrobiologyNotes
Type IPolymicrobial (gram-positive, gram-negative, anaerobes)Most common (~55–75%); often diabetic, post-surgical, immunocompromised
Type IIMonomicrobial — most often Group A streptococcus (or S. aureus including MRSA)Rapidly progressive; "flesh-eating" presentation; often previously healthy individuals
Type IIIVibrio vulnificus (also Aeromonas hydrophila)Salt-water exposure; rapid progression; highly lethal (~40-50%)
Type IVFungal (e.g., Mucor)Immunocompromised; high mortality

Specific Syndromes

  • Fournier's gangrene — necrotizing fasciitis of perineum/genital area; classically polymicrobial in elderly diabetic males.
  • Ludwig's angina — submandibular/sublingual space infection; airway compromise.
  • Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome — Group A strep + invasive disease + multiorgan failure + hypotension.
  • Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) — C. perfringens; crepitus + brown discharge + extreme tachycardia.

Risk Factors

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Alcoholism, IV drug use, immunocompromise
  • Peripheral vascular disease
  • Recent surgery or trauma
  • Salt-water exposure (Vibrio)
  • Cirrhosis
  • NSAID use (debated — may mask early symptoms)

Clinical Features (high index of suspicion)

  • Pain out of proportion to exam findings — classic early feature.
  • Triad: severe pain + swelling + fever.
  • Hard signs (late): crepitus, hemorrhagic/violaceous bullae, skin necrosis, anesthesia of the affected area, systemic toxicity, rapid progression (1 inch/h).
  • Discoloration: erythema → dusky → purple/bluish → black necrosis.
  • Mental status changes, hypotension, multi-organ failure as it progresses.
📚 Fig 152-6 — Necrotizing soft tissue infection: large hemorrhagic bullae with dark purple fluid on the leg (Tintinalli p.1011)
⚠️ Mortality without prompt surgery: NSTI mortality approaches 20–40% even with treatment; nearly 100% without surgical debridement. The single most important prognostic factor is time to operative debridement.
Inline MCQ 5. Which clinical feature is the most useful EARLY warning sign for necrotizing fasciitis?

Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Pain out of proportion to physical findings
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Hemorrhagic bullae
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Skin necrosis
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Hard signs (crepitus, bullae, necrosis) are LATE. Early recognition relies on disproportionate pain. Reference: Tintinalli p.1011.

8. LRINEC Score for Necrotizing Fasciitis

Tintinalli Table 152-6 p.1011

LRINEC = Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis. Score ≥6 raises suspicion, ≥8 strongly predictive. Caveat: a low LRINEC does NOT rule out NSTI in patients with concerning clinical features.

VariableThresholdPoints
CRP>150 mg/L+4
WBC15–25 × 10³/µL
>25 × 10³/µL		+1
+2
Hemoglobin11–13.5 g/dL
<11 g/dL		+1
+2
Sodium<135 mmol/L+2
Creatinine>1.6 mg/dL+2
Glucose>180 mg/dL+1

Interpretation: Score 0–5 = low risk · 6–7 = intermediate · ≥8 = high risk.

📚 Table 152-6 — Laboratory & Imaging Findings Associated with Necrotizing Fasciitis (Tintinalli p.1011)

Imaging

  • Plain X-ray: gas in soft tissues — highly specific (when present), but poor sensitivity.
  • CT with contrast: deep fascial gas, fluid along fascial planes, non-enhancing fascia. AKI and contrast risk should be considered but not delay surgery if clinical suspicion high.
  • MRI: most sensitive but rarely available in real time; cannot delay OR.
  • Bedside US: can show subcutaneous gas, but not validated.
⚠️ Pearl — surgery beats imaging: if NSTI is strongly suspected, the patient goes to OR. Don't delay debridement to "rule out" with imaging.
Inline MCQ 6. Which LRINEC score threshold is associated with HIGH risk of necrotizing fasciitis?
A. ≥3
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. ≥5
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. ≥8
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. ≥12
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. ≥6 = intermediate, ≥8 = high risk. Note clinical judgment supersedes the score. Reference: Tintinalli Table 152-6.

9. NSTI Management

Tintinalli p.1011

The 4 pillars

  1. Aggressive resuscitation — fluids, vasopressors as needed, sepsis bundle (cross-reference Ch.151).
  2. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics — within 1 h:
    • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h OR meropenem 1 g IV q8h
    • + Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV (MRSA/group A strep coverage)
    • + Clindamycin 600–900 mg IV q8h (toxin suppression — Eagle effect)
    • For Vibrio (saltwater exposure): add doxycycline 100 mg IV q12h + ceftriaxone
  3. Source control — surgical debridement as soon as possible:
    • Single most important prognostic factor.
    • Multiple operative procedures often required.
    • "Look-back" debridement at 24–48 h.
  4. Adjuncts (selective use):
    • Hyperbaric oxygen (clostridial myonecrosis, Fournier's): controversial.
    • IVIG for streptococcal TSS.
    • Aggressive metabolic and hemodynamic support.
Why clindamycin in NSTI?
• Suppresses bacterial protein synthesis (toxin production from Group A strep, S. aureus).
• Effective against high-inoculum infections where β-lactams are less effective ("Eagle effect").
• Anaerobic coverage.
Inline MCQ 7. A patient with rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis. Which is the SINGLE most important prognostic intervention?
A. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Maximum-dose vancomycin
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Early surgical debridement
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. IVIG
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. Time to surgical debridement is the strongest predictor of survival. Antibiotics alone are inadequate. Reference: Tintinalli p.1011.

10. Disposition

Tintinalli p.1010
  • Discharge home: simple cellulitis or small abscess after I&D, ambulatory, no systemic toxicity, reliable follow-up at 24–48 h.
  • Admit (general ward): systemic symptoms, immunocompromised, comorbidities (DM, hemodialysis, IVDU), failed outpatient therapy, rapidly progressive.
  • ICU: NSTI, Fournier's, septic shock from SSTI, toxic shock syndrome, severe metabolic derangement.
  • OR: NSTI, deep abscess requiring complex drainage.
  • Specialty consultation: ENT for deep neck, urology for Fournier's, plastic surgery for facial sites.

⚕️ ATLS 11th — Soft Tissue Infections in Trauma

ATLS
  • Suspect NSTI in trauma patients with rapidly worsening pain, dusky discoloration, hemorrhagic bullae at injury site, particularly with delayed presentation.
  • Penetrating wounds with foreign body retention or contamination by soil/saltwater warrant prophylactic broad coverage.
  • Crush injuries can mimic clostridial myonecrosis early — both have crepitus and pain out of proportion. Confirm with imaging and look for systemic signs.
  • Tetanus prophylaxis per immunization status for any wound.
  • Source control via debridement remains primary; antibiotics are adjunct.
  • Surgical fascial assessment ("finger test" or biopsy) is sometimes necessary when imaging is equivocal — direct exploration in OR is gold standard.
Rosen Source Check: Rosen is used to cross-check ED severity flags, necrotizing infection pitfalls, ultrasound use, and disposition thresholds. Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli supplies tables and chapter structure; Rosen adds bedside diagnostic nuance and escalation triggers.

📗 Rosen's EM 10th — Soft Tissue Infections

Rosen's Ch.124
  • Same general framework as Tintinalli on cellulitis vs erysipelas vs NSTI.
  • Rosen's emphasis: POCUS for suspected abscess routinely (improves I&D yield and reduces missed abscesses).
  • Loop drainage technique discussed as effective alternative to traditional packing for simple abscesses — less pain, comparable cure.
  • Antibiotic adjunct after I&D: Rosen's cites recent RCTs (Talan et al, NEJM 2016) supporting TMP-SMX adjunct improves cure, particularly for abscesses ≥2 cm.
  • NSTI: stresses the futility of waiting for imaging when clinical features are concerning — direct OR exploration ("finger test") is acceptable.
  • Vibrio NSTI: emphasizes saltwater exposure and rapid progression; specific antibiotic doxycycline + ceftriaxone or cefotaxime preferred.

Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Pip-tazo + vancomycin + clindamycin IV
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Ceftriaxone IV alone
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. TMP-SMX PO
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Diabetic foot NSTI is polymicrobial — needs broad-spectrum + MRSA + toxin suppression.
End MCQ 20. Which finding strongly suggests clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene)?
A. Slow progression
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Crepitus + brown 'dishwater' discharge + extreme tachycardia disproportionate to fever
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Localized erythema only
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Absence of pain
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. Gas gangrene: crepitus, dishwater discharge, tachycardia disproportionate to fever, rapid progression.

🔑 Key Points (High-Yield)

  1. Cellulitis vs Erysipelas: erysipelas has sharp demarcation + lymphatic involvement; cellulitis has indistinct edges + deeper.
  2. Purulent SSTI = empirically MRSA — TMP-SMX or doxycycline (mild), vanco (severe).
  3. Non-purulent = streptococcal — cephalexin (mild), cefazolin/ceftriaxone (severe).
  4. I&D is the cornerstone for cutaneous abscess; adjunctive antibiotics if ≥2 cm or surrounding cellulitis.
  5. POCUS first-line bedside imaging for suspected abscess.
  6. NSTI early signs: pain out of proportion to exam + triad of severe pain/swelling/fever. Hard signs (crepitus, bullae, necrosis) are LATE.
  7. LRINEC: CRP, WBC, Hgb, Na, Cr, glucose. ≥8 = high risk. Score supports — clinical judgment supersedes.
  8. NSTI antibiotics = Pip-tazo + Vanco + Clindamycin (toxin suppression).
  9. NSTI management: Resuscitation + Antibiotics + SURGERY + Adjuncts. Time to OR = #1 prognostic factor.
  10. Vibrio NSTI in saltwater exposure → add doxycycline + ceftriaxone.
  11. Fournier's gangrene = NSTI of perineum/genitals, often elderly diabetic males.
  12. Don't drain pulsatile masses, deep neck, periorbital regions in ED — get specialist.
